title: Breach clocks: CERT-In 6 hours, DPDP, RBI and GDPR
summary: Rehearse a personal-data breach at a microfinance company after India's DPDP breach rules take effect: start the clock, scope the breach from the logs, file with CERT-In inside six hours while injects arrive, work out every other clock that applies (RBI, DPDP, GDPR), and write the Board note, the notice to customers and the notification order.
handin: A filed CERT-In report and its update, a DPDP notification pack (Board note and the notice to the people affected), and a one-page notification order.
rubric: Clock started at the right moment, with the evidence for it
Scope measured from the logs: requests, records and countries
CERT-In report filed within six hours: right type, indicators, systems and actions
Inbox answered and an update sent with the new facts
Notification order: every clock that applies, in order, each with an owner
DPDP pack: the Board note and the plain-language notice, with every required part
Plain writing: facts kept apart from guesses

script.intro: Welcome to Breach clocks. This is a rehearsal set in June 2027, after India's new data protection breach rules have started. Kaveri Microfinance runs a loan app, and this morning its security team found that someone pulled thousands of customers' records out of the app's API. From the moment they noticed, clocks are running: CERT-In, the Reserve Bank, the Data Protection Board, and for a few customers, Europe. Today you'll start the clock, scope the breach, file on time while new facts arrive, and write what each reader needs.
script.outro: That's the morning at Kaveri. The clock started at 04:50 UTC, the CERT-In and RBI reports went in before 10:50, the update followed the new facts, the Board note went out at once, and customers got a notice in words they can use. The detailed report to the Data Protection Board is due within 72 hours, and Ireland's regulator gets its own. Next is seminar seven: identity, where most of these breaches begin.
steps: Every clock starts when you noticed. The scraping began at 08:40 India time, but nobody knew. The analyst noticed at 10:20 India time, 04:50 UTC. That's the start. Six hours later, 10:50 UTC, is when CERT-In and the Reserve Bank must have their reports. Write both time zones down; people will mix them up all morning.

Now how much. The scraper made 2060 requests, each for a different customer, one every two seconds, from 08:40 to 09:48 India time: 03:10 to 04:18 UTC. Normal app traffic asks for the signed-in customer's own record. This client had one customer's token and walked through everyone else's IDs. That's a missing ownership check.

To whom. Counting by country: 1932 in India, 64 in the UAE, 41 in Germany and 23 in Ireland. Every record has a name, mobile number, loan amount, the last four digits of Aadhaar and an address. That's enough for convincing fraud calls. And 64 people in the EU means GDPR may apply too.

File now, with what we know. The form checks the detection time against the evidence, the type, and whether indicators, systems and actions are filled in. Data breach is the type. We file at 08:15 UTC, well inside six hours. Then the inbox: CERT-In asks for logs, the CISO says the flaw is three weeks old and fixed, and the press office has a journalist on the line. The update goes to CERT-In quoting the reference.

CERT-In is only the first clock. The tool's clock panel shows the rest: the Reserve Bank, also six hours; the Data Protection Board and every affected customer, without delay; the detailed report to the Board within 72 hours; and if GDPR applies, the Irish regulator within 72 hours. One page, one owner per row, every time in UTC.

Now the people. The CEO wants to wait for the root cause; we file on time with partial facts. The DPO asks about customers; they're told today in plain words. The journalist gets a short honest confirmation, after the regulators and customers. And the 64 people in Europe mean we check GDPR rather than ignore it.

Two more readers. The Board note starts with the ask: approve fraud alerts for a year and an outside review. The notice to customers is the hardest writing of the day. What happened, what they saw, what could happen, what we did, what you can do, and a person to call. No jargon, and no line about taking privacy seriously. Read it aloud. If your grandmother couldn't act on it, rewrite it.
Hand in the notebook: the CERT-In filing and update, the notification order, the Board note, the customer notice and your tabletop path. The rubric is on screen.
